facts.fact_text: On 1 April 2013 Mr Frolov submitted a notification to the prefecture of the Severo-Vostochnyy District in Moscow, stating his intention to hold, on 13 April 2013, a 'meeting to promote the teaching of Vaishnavism and a healthy lifestyle based on spiritual values', with up to fifteen people participating.

On 2 April 2013 the prefecture of the Severo-Vostochnyy District in Moscow rejected Mr Frolov's notification on the grounds that 'the stated purpose – promoting the teaching of Vaishnavism – does not correspond to section 2(1) of the Public Events Act (Law no. 54-FZ of 19 June 2004)'.

On 2 April 2013 the prefecture of the Severo-Vostochnyy District in Moscow rejected Mr Frolov's notification on the grounds that 'the stated purpose – promoting the teaching of Vaishnavism – does not correspond to section 2(1) of the Public Events Act (Law no. 54-FZ of 19 June 2004)'.
On 12 August 2013 the Meshchanskiy District Court in Moscow pronounced the prefecture's refusal of Mr Frolov's first notification to have been lawful and justified.

The Meshchanskiy District Court in Moscow found on 12 August 2013 that the promotion of the teaching of Vaishnavism did not correspond to the purposes of a public event listed in section 2(1) of the Public Events Act (Law no. 54-FZ of 19 June 2004).
On 16 January 2014 the Moscow City Court dismissed Mr Frolov's appeal against the Meshchanskiy District Court's decision of 12 August 2013.
The Moscow City Court found on 16 January 2014 that 'the missionary activities, of which Mr Frolov had informed the prefecture, did not correspond to the lawful purposes of a public event'.
The Moscow City Court found on 16 January 2014 that Mr Frolov's missionary activities were 'incompatible with the respect for the religious beliefs of others'.
The Moscow City Court found on 16 January 2014 that 'the rejection of the notification of a public event was therefore lawful'.
On 20 April 2013 a few participants gathered at the designated location of the religious event planned by Mr Frolov.
On 20 April 2013 a police officer told the participants who had gathered at the designated location of Mr Frolov's religious event to disperse.

The Religions Act (Law no. 125-FZ of 26 September 1997) established that in cases other than those covered by section 16 subsections 2, 3 and 4, public services of worship, religious rites and ceremonies were to be conducted in accordance with the procedure established for conducting meetings, marches and demonstrations (section 16, subsection 5).

Section 1(2) of the Public Events Act (Law no. 54-FZ of 19 June 2004) establishes that the conduct of 'religious rites and ceremonies' is governed by the Religions Act (Law no. 125-FZ of 26 September 1997).
On 1 November 2008 the official website of the Governor and Government of the Ulyanovsk Region announced that the project 'Beware: cults!' (Осторожно – секты!) was moving forward.
The chief objective of the project 'Beware: cults!' was stated to be the 'prevention of negative activities of destructive religious groups in the region'.
The project 'Beware: cults!' had begun in April 2008 with a conference co-organised by the Government of the Ulyanovsk Region and the Ulyanovsk State University.
An action plan adopted at the conference co-organised by the Government of the Ulyanovsk Region and the Ulyanovsk State University had included the setting-up of an anti-cult hot line.

An action plan adopted at the conference co-organised by the Government of the Ulyanovsk Region and the Ulyanovsk State University had included the organisation of roundtables and seminars with the participation of youth organisations, ministers of 'traditional denominations', authorities, educators and members of the public.
An educational seminar titled 'Adverse effects of cults on the minds of children and youth' had been held on 31 October 2008.
At the educational seminar held on 31 October 2008, vice-principals of secondary schools, teaching staff, and religious ministers had discussed the religious situation in the Ulyanovsk Region.
At the educational seminar held on 31 October 2008, teaching staff had been given pamphlets, posters and brochures to be distributed among their students.

The brochure 'Watch out for cults!' (Будьте внимательны: секты!) had been compiled in the framework of the project 'Beware: cults!' by experts of the Government of the Ulyanovsk Region together with staff of the Ulyanovsk State University.

The first deputy chief of staff of the Government of the Ulyanovsk Region was quoted as saying: 'the Government attaches particular importance to ... the protection of the population from the influence of totalitarian cults'.
An electronic version of the brochure 'Watch out for cults!' was published on the Ulyanovsk regional Government's website.
The cover page of the brochure 'Watch out for cults!' listed 'Government of the Ulyanovsk Region' and 'Ulyanovsk State University' at the top, followed by the names of three authors.
The second page of the brochure 'Watch out for cults!' stated that the methodical recommendations had been compiled on the basis of works by prominent Russian and international religious scholars.

The second page of the brochure 'Watch out for cults!' stated that the methodical recommendations were addressed to administrators of educational institutions and officials in charge of education in the matter of destructive activities of totalitarian cults in the Ulyanovsk Region.
The second page of the brochure 'Watch out for cults!' stated that it was published by decision of the Government of the Ulyanovsk Region.

Chapter 2 of the brochure 'Watch out for cults!' provided an overview of 'non-traditional religious movements active in the Ulyanovsk Region', including Jehovah's Witnesses, Mormons, Unification Church of Rev. Moon, Scientology, and Krishna Society.

The section on the Krishna Society in the brochure 'Watch out for cults!' described members of the International Society for Krishna Consciousness as 'flamboyant groups of mostly young people dressed in white and yellow garments who sing unintelligible hymns to the beat of drums and other musical instruments'.
The section on the Krishna Society in the brochure 'Watch out for cults!' described the International Society for Krishna Consciousness as a 'totalitarian cult'.
The section on the Krishna Society in the brochure 'Watch out for cults!' described the life of the founder of the Krishna Societies, the precepts of the faith, rituals and dietary restrictions.
The section on the Krishna Society in the brochure 'Watch out for cults!' stated that 'the goals of Krishnaites are frequently rather materialistic: they seek to obtain money by all means'.

The section on the Krishna Society in the brochure 'Watch out for cults!' stated that Krishnaites 'beg for money in the street, they sell their literature; in some countries, they have been caught stealing or selling drugs'.
The section on the Krishna Society in the brochure 'Watch out for cults!' stated that money obtained by Krishnaites 'goes to the leaders of the cult who keep a close watch on that activity'.
The section on the Krishna Society in the brochure 'Watch out for cults!' concluded that 'this religious movement is highly destructive for our society'.

The section on the Krishna Society in the brochure 'Watch out for cults!' stated that the Krishna movement 'has no genetic, historic or geographic connection to our people' and is 'a peculiar spiritual culture of the East'.
The section on the Krishna Society in the brochure 'Watch out for cults!' stated that 'zombification and psychological manipulation of our youth constitute a serious threat to our future'.

On 29 December 2008 the Ulyanovsk regional prosecutor's office replied that the State authorities had carried out the project 'Beware: cults!' within their legal authority.

On 29 December 2008 the Ulyanovsk regional prosecutor's office replied that the primary objective of the project 'Beware: cults!' had been to discuss matters relating to an interfaith dialogue and build the best possible framework for a relationship between the State and religious organisations.

On 29 December 2008 the Ulyanovsk regional prosecutor's office replied that the brochure 'Watch out for cults!' had been developed by staff of the Ulyanovsk State University and presented a variety of views on the activities of 'non-traditional religious organisations'.

On 29 December 2008 the Ulyanovsk regional prosecutor's office advised the Centre of Societies for Krishna Consciousness in Russia that if they believed their rights had been violated, they should apply to a court for protection.
Further hierarchical appeals by the Centre of Societies for Krishna Consciousness in Russia following the Ulyanovsk regional prosecutor's office reply elicited similar responses.
The Centre of Societies for Krishna Consciousness in Russia turned to a court for substantive review of the prosecutors' decisions after further hierarchical appeals elicited similar responses.

On 27 October 2010 the Tverskoy District Court in Moscow held that the prosecutors had considered all the matters which the Centre of Societies for Krishna Consciousness in Russia had complained about and gave sufficient responses.

The Tverskoy District Court in Moscow held on 27 October 2010 that the Centre of Societies for Krishna Consciousness in Russia's disagreement with the contents of the prosecutors' responses did not constitute a sufficient reason to impugn them.
On 16 March 2011 the Moscow City Court upheld the Tverskoy District Court's judgment of 27 October 2010 on appeal.
The first applicant, the Centre of Societies for Krishna Consciousness in Russia (Центр обществ сознания Кришны в России), is a centralised religious organisation.
The Centre of Societies for Krishna Consciousness in Russia was established under Russian law on religious associations in 1992.
The Centre of Societies for Krishna Consciousness in Russia has its registered office in Moscow.
The second applicant, Mr Frolov, was born in 1975.
Mr Frolov lives in the Moscow Region.
The applicants were represented before the Court by Mr V. Borisov, vice-president of the Centre of Societies for Krishna Consciousness in Russia.
The applicants were represented before the Court by Mr S. Minenkov, a lawyer practising in Moscow.
The Government were initially represented by Mr M. Galperin, former Representative of the Russian Federation to the European Court of Human Rights.
The Government were later represented by Mr M. Vinogradov, successor to Mr M. Galperin as Representative of the Russian Federation to the European Court of Human Rights.
